records.name: Aruba
records.summary:
An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.

sources.claim: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

records.name: Afghanistan
records.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. The 2024 Morality Law (PVPV) obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism"; the Taliban applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender Afghans report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that UN experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.

sources.claim: EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (updated Jan 19, 2026): Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Penal Code 2017 provisions on 'sodomy' and 'inciting sodomy' carry up to two years, while the Penal Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty for same-sex activity.
CNN (Nov 2024): 'LGBTQ Afghans say they face abuse in detention as Taliban crackdown intensifies' — first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

records.name: Angola
records.summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

sources.claim: Shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session (Oct-Nov 2024, Banjul) by Angolan organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others) with ILGA/Synergia support: documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people in Angola.

Submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights pre-session (74th, review of Angola): foregrounds the Angolan context for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people ahead of the state's review — a formal international-review channel raising discrimination and health-access issues.

Southern Africa Litigation Centre chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola': maps constitutional protection gaps — Article 23 does not list gender or sexual orientation as prohibited discrimination grounds — and locates identity, privacy, liberty, torture-protection and expression rights across Title II articles of the Angolan Constitution.

VICE continental overview (Oct 28, 2019): Angola singled out as having gone furthest among African reforms — not only removing the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision but also criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services; contrasts legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

BBC profile (Apr 12, 2012): kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becomes a mainstream star at 25 in what the article describes as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour — evidence of visible trans presence alongside formal criminalisation at that time.

PinkNews (Feb 11, 2021): Angola's decriminalisation took effect on this date — the law adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era ban describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and made discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds punishable by prison.

records.name: Anguilla
records.summary:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance; the earlier profile's 'decriminalised 2019' appeared in no source and has been deleted. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies — useful as a practical marker that only symbolic ceremonies are possible for same-sex couples there.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

records.name: Albania
records.summary:
Albania is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.

sources.claim: End-of-mission statement of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity after the country visit to Albania, 1-12 July 2024: assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the State — the international-review baseline for Albanian SOGI conditions.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) Albania chapter: discrimination complaints filed over the film 'Strange World' screenings were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour in one case; Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 (17 Jun 2025) by Independent Expert Graeme Reid on the Albania visit of 1-12 Jul 2024: evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

PinkNews (Feb 5, 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as EU-integration driven.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work under the Berisha-led opposition.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): MP Nard Ndoka's Facebook post branding the government 'LGBT' and accusing it of pushing LGBT values in schools, illustrating political anti-LGBT messaging in the same week as the schools campaign row.

Balkan Insight (Oct 27, 2011): Albania's Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community.

records.name: Andorra
records.summary:
Andorra is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. Gaps: anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity is recent and shallower than Spain's; hate-crime law is generic rather than SOGI-specific. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Andorra chapter: a transphobic opinion piece in El Periòdic d'Andorra (27 Sep) was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd's request though it had already run in print; in August DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for gender-affirming protocols — puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, in some cases 14 — following the 2022 regulatory changes.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025), Andorra chapter: Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month; DiversAnd flagged incidents during June Pride celebrations and called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so it can be recognised as hate crime; the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during the year.

PinkNews (Sep 12, 2023): Andorra's head of government Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly saying 'I never hid it' — a societal-climate signal for a country where he remains the serving prime minister.

GayLawNet Andorra laws page: age of consent is 16 under Penal Code Article 206, with topic coverage including civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status; marked 'limited information', useful as a dated legal-index pointer rather than analysis.

records.name: United Arab Emirates
records.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.

sources.claim: Ynetnews (2025): two Israeli trans women describe being detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched their female passport records, mocked by staff, and denied entry with passports confiscated — a direct visitor-experience account of gender-document screening at UAE entry.

VICE (Mar 21, 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon (2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up) was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before her Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

Metropoles (Apr 2023, Portuguese): a Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE since September 2022 — arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test — accused the consulate of negligence; a documented case of a trans foreigner in prolonged UAE custody.

Cairo 52 legal review of the United Arab Emirates: the UAE employs various legal mechanisms that explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles; transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion — the legal-framework basis for visitor risk.

Outright International UAE country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): a new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (Article 409 also covers unmarried different-sex couples); charges require a complaint basis; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

TMZ (Aug 9, 2016): trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport, headlined as 'Dubai won't let me in because I'm transgender' — an early high-profile case of a trans visitor refused UAE entry on identity grounds.

records.name: Argentina
records.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (Apr 10, 2025): interviews in Buenos Aires (Apr 4, 2025) with trans activists — including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán (stabbed to death 2015) and Lohana Berkins — saying President Milei's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

Agencia Presentes (Mar 19, 2026): the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Agencia Presentes (Feb 6, 2025): President Milei's government issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it pertains to minors, plus another decree on housing of transgender people in prisons; legal experts call the decree illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Argentina's decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors.

Outright International Argentina overview (updated Mar 12, 2026): Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality (2010) and passed one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws in 2012 allowing legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval; anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws — while the page's at-a-glance panel reports current negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration under review.

misterb&b Buenos Aires safety guide (updated May 28, 2026): first-person account of walking Buenos Aires at every hour, giving practical gay-traveler safety impressions for the Argentine capital — commercial gay-travel guide, useful as a recent on-the-ground visitor perspective.

Wikipedia, Gender Identity Law (Argentina), Law 26,743: approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated 24 May 2012; lauded by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region; allows legal gender change without surgery or court approval.

Infobae (Apr 5, 2025): Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino, convicted of the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020 — meaning the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied.
